content.title: About
content.content: Biscuit is a light, airy baked good made from flour, eggs, sugar and a small amount of fat. It is commonly served in fast‑food outlets and restaurants as a standalone dessert, a cake base, or as a sandwich with various fillings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Biscuit originated in Europe in the 19th century as a lighter alternative to traditional cakes.
Traditional biscuit contains no leavening agents; its fluffiness comes from whipped egg whites.
In some countries the biscuit is called “soft” because of its tender texture.
Biscuit is often used as a base for mille‑feuille and trifle desserts.
Both sweet and savory versions exist, served with sauces, fruit, or simply dusted with powdered sugar.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Biscuit usually contains less fat than many other baked goods, making it a lighter snack option.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: It provides a quick source of energy through simple carbohydrates.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Eggs in the recipe add a modest amount of plant‑based protein.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: Its airy structure allows rapid digestion, suitable for a light bite.

items.title: Can be fortified
items.content: Recipes often incorporate fruit purées or nuts, boosting vitamin and mineral content.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Biscuit is typically made with wheat flour, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Sugar and simple carbs may cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes, so those with diabetes should limit portions.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Traditional biscuits are often sweet, contributing to dental decay and weight gain when consumed excessively.

items.title: Preservatives in commercial versions
items.content: Store‑bought biscuits may contain additives and preservatives that are not suitable for sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Biscuit can be enjoyed on its own, sliced and served with berry sauce, used as a cake layer, made into sandwiches with ham, cheese or vegetables, or toasted for a crisp crust.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep biscuits in an airtight container at room temperature, away from direct light. For longer storage place them in the refrigerator, and for several months store them in the freezer. Before eating, check for any mold or off‑odors.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide. It belongs to the bird family Phasianidae. The meat is tender, has a mild flavor, and contains less fat than most red meats. Chicken is used in countless cuisines, from simple roasts to sophisticated gourmet dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken is the most consumed meat globally.
Chicken breast is often called “white meat,” while thigh is considered “dark meat.”
Chicken skin can be rendered to make rich stocks and sauces because it is high in collagen.
Different cultures have signature chicken dishes: fried chicken in the USA, tandoori chicken in India, chicken kebabs in the Middle East.
Commercial poultry farms control temperature, lighting, and feed to optimize growth.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Skin‑less breast meat is especially low in saturated fat, making it suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Rich in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, chicken supports metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Chicken supplies phosphorus, selenium, and zinc, important for bones, immunity, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Selenium and vitamin B6 help maintain a healthy immune response.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may contain Salmonella or Campylobacter; it must be cooked to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Processed chicken products (e.g., deli meats, smoked chicken) often contain high levels of salt.

items.title: Antibiotics and hormones
items.content: In some regions, poultry may be raised with antibiotics; choose certified or organic sources when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chicken can be grilled, baked, boiled, stewed, fried, or used in soups and salads. Breast meat is popular in low‑fat dishes, while thighs add richness to stews. Chicken broth forms the base for many sauces and soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh chicken should be kept in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Frozen chicken can be stored for up to 9 months at –18 °C (0 °F). Thaw frozen meat in the fridge before cooking. Discard any chicken that has an off‑odor or discoloration.

chicken-breast-baked-coated-skin-coating.title: Chicken breast, baked, coated, skin/coating not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken breast is a lean, boneless cut of meat rich in protein. In this form it is baked, coated with a breading, and the skin and coating are not consumed. This preparation retains most nutrients while providing a convenient, ready‑to‑eat option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken breast provides about 31 g of protein per 100 g.
Baking without added fat makes it more diet‑friendly than frying.
The coating is often made from whole‑grain flour or breadcrumbs, adding a small amount of carbs and fiber.
Chicken is a good source of vitamin B6, which supports amino‑acid metabolism.
When baked at 180 °C the breast stays moist and juicy.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Protein is essential for muscle growth, repair, and immune function.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: Skin‑less baked breast contains little saturated fat, supporting heart health.

items.title: Vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 aids protein metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: With minimal carbohydrates, it does not cause rapid blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Salmonella risk
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor harmful bacteria; ensure proper cooking temperature.

items.title: Sodium in the coating
items.content: Prepared breadings often contain salt; choose low‑sodium versions if needed.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Some ready‑made coatings may include preservatives or flavor enhancers that not everyone tolerates.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the breast and add it to salads, sandwiches, or wraps. It works well in quick meals such as pasta, rice bowls, or vegetable stir‑fries. If the coating is not edible, remove it before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked breast in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags at –18 °C, where it remains good for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 75 °C before eating.

chocolate-milk-reduced-sugar-fat-free-sk.title: Chocolate Milk, Reduced Sugar, Fat Free (Skim)

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑sugar, fat‑free chocolate milk is a beverage made from skim cow’s milk, cocoa powder and low‑calorie sweeteners, providing a chocolate flavor with less sugar and virtually no fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Skim milk retains most nutrients while containing almost no fat.
Sugar reduction is achieved with stevia or erythritol, which do not raise blood glucose.
The cocoa used is rich in flavonoids, known for antioxidant properties.
Athletes and calorie‑conscious consumers often choose this drink.
In many markets it is sold in 250 ml and 1 L cartons.

items.title: High in calcium
items.content: Skim milk provides a substantial amount of calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of fat makes the drink suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Reduced sugar
items.content: Lower sugar content helps maintain stable blood glucose levels, beneficial for those with pre‑diabetes.

items.title: Cocoa antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids from cocoa may support cardiovascular health and improve mood.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Milk supplies high‑quality dairy protein that aids tissue repair and satiety.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Skim milk contains lactose; individuals with intolerance should opt for lactose‑free versions.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergic reactions to casein or whey can occur in sensitive people.

items.title: Artificial sweeteners
items.content: Some sweeteners may cause gastrointestinal discomfort when consumed in large amounts.

items.title: Caffeine content
items.content: Cocoa contains a small amount of theobromine, which can affect sleep in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink it chilled as a refreshing beverage, blend into smoothies, use as a base for protein shakes, or add to oatmeal and cereals for a chocolate flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 1 °C–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days. Do not freeze, as texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: Halibut (Hippoglossus) is a large flatfish of the family Pleuronectidae, found in the cold northern waters of the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. It has firm, white, mildly sweet flesh, low fat content, and a distinctive flattened body. Halibut is prized in cuisine for baking, grilling, poaching, and sushi.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Halibut can grow over 2.5 m in length and weigh more than 300 kg.
It is one of the most valuable commercial fish species, valued for its delicate flavor and texture.
Halibut changes sex during its life: younger individuals are males, older ones become females.
In the wild, halibut can live up to 50 years.
Its flesh contains lower mercury levels compared with many other large marine fish.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Halibut provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many fish, halibut has a low fat content, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of omega‑3
items.content: Despite its low fat, halibut still supplies beneficial omega‑3 fatty acids that support heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It is rich in B12, B6, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Halibut contains selenium, phosphorus, and potassium, nutrients important for immunity, bone health, and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including halibut.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Although mercury levels are generally low, choose fish from reputable sources, especially for children and pregnant women.

items.title: Possible parasites
items.content: Raw or undercooked fish can harbor parasites; proper cooking eliminates this risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Halibut is excellent baked in foil with lemon and herbs, pan‑seared, poached in broth, or used for sushi. The fillets can be cut into cubes for salads, soups, or stews.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh halibut should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C and used within 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag at –18 °C; thaw in the refrigerator before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned lentils are a ready‑to‑eat product made from selected lentil varieties that are pre‑cooked and sealed in airtight cans. They have a mild nutty flavor, a tender texture, and retain most of their nutrients thanks to rapid heat processing.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lentils are one of the oldest legume crops, cultivated for over 8,000 years.
A typical 400 g can contains roughly 20 g of plant protein.
Canned lentils preserve nearly all B‑vitamins, iron, and dietary fiber.
They are easily digestible and suitable for vegetarians and vegans.
Canned lentils are popular in camping and emergency food supplies because of their long shelf life.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Lentils provide about 9 g of protein per 100 g, making them a valuable plant‑based protein source.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These micronutrients are essential for blood formation and anemia prevention, especially in women of childbearing age.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Lentils raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for people with pre‑diabetes or diabetes.

items.title: Source of magnesium and potassium
items.content: These minerals aid heart, muscle, and nervous system function.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned foods often contain added salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you need to limit sodium intake.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to lentils.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Legumes can cause increased gas in some people; start with small portions.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some brands add preservatives; opt for products without additives if you are sensitive.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned lentils can be eaten straight from the can, added to salads, soups, stews, pasta dishes, or used as a sandwich filling. Rinsing them briefly with cold water before use can reduce excess salt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, transfer lentils to an airtight container and keep refrigerated for 3–4 days.
